passage:
Monday: Rajni's physics mock came back with 38 out of 100. That night she stayed at her desk until the window turned grey, reading the same three chapters again and again.

Wednesday: Jahnavi found her in the corridor, eyes red, and asked for the formula sheet Rajni had promised. Rajni could not remember where a motion problem even started. "Stop asking me things!" she snapped. She had spent a second night awake.

Friday: In the class test, her mind went blank at question two. Afterwards she counted on her fingers: eleven extra hours gained, and she had forgotten more than she had learned. Jahnavi sat beside her with a bottle of water and said nothing for a while.

qa.q: How many marks did Rajni score in the physics mock?
What was Rajni feeling when 'Stop asking me things!' came out, and what suggests it?
qa.a: Rajni was frazzled, anxious and short of sleep; the red eyes and forgetting a problem after a night at the desk suggest it.

qa.q: What approach to the last month could work better than all-nighters, and why?
qa.a: A steady schedule with fixed sleep and a mock paper marked for weak topics would work better, because a rested memory holds what was studied.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi see Rajni's late-night plan?
qa.a: Jahnavi sees a friend worn out and struggling, so Jahnavi offers water and quiet company instead of arguing. 🤍

grounding: Anxiety after a bad mock pushes the student into all-nighters, and two nights of poor sleep cost her memory and mood, erasing the extra hours.

passage: Harsha, your Devika Maasi has a confession, from the month before my boards. I had just got 38 out of 100 in the pre-board Maths mock. I was so frightened that I decided sleep was for people who had done well. Two nights in a row I sat at my desk with the tube light buzzing, working sums till the birds started. My mother kept coming in with milk and going out again, worried. The next days were a blur. I forgot formulas I'd known for years. I cried in the school bus because a friend said good morning too loudly. When I did the next practice paper, I got 36. Two nights of no sleep, and I had lost two marks, not gained any.

qa.q: What did young Devika score in the pre-board Maths mock?
What feeling pushed young Devika to study through the night?
qa.a: Young Devika was frightened after the bad mock and anxious to make up for it at any cost.

qa.q: Which choice in the story could have changed the next paper?
qa.a: Sleeping normally after the bad mock and working on weak topics by day, since the all-nighters wiped out memory and mood.

qa.q: How might Devika's mother have felt during those nights?
qa.a: She seems worried, coming in with milk and going out again, unsure how to help her frightened daughter.

grounding: An elder recalls panic after a bad mock leading to all-nighters that hurt memory and mood and cancelled the extra hours.

passage: The Physics board paper was six days away when Dolma's mock came back: 29 out of 70. That night, in the small room she shared with her brother Chetan in their Darjeeling flat, she decided to study straight through. Chetan grumbled about the lamp and pulled the quilt over his head. By four in the morning she had done three chapters and felt almost proud. The next day she dozed on the school bus, snapped at her best friend for asking about lunch, and couldn't remember a formula she had revised at two. So she stayed up again, to make up for the lost day. On the third morning, working a practice paper, she stared at a question on lenses she knew she had done twice. Nothing came. Two nights of extra hours, and she remembered less than before.

qa.q: What did Dolma score in the mock?
What was Dolma feeling when she snapped at her best friend?
qa.a: She was exhausted and irritable, her mood worn down by a night without sleep.

qa.q: What else could Dolma have done after the bad mock?
qa.a: Used the next days on the topics the mock showed as weak, while keeping normal sleep so memory and mood stayed intact.

qa.q: What are Dolma's all-nighters like for Chetan?
qa.a: Chetan loses sleep to the lamp and grumbles, and may worry seeing his sister so tired and snappy.

grounding: Shows a student reacting to a bad mock with two all-nighters, damaging memory and mood so the extra hours are lost.
